question: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 into an empty BST. What is its inorder traversal?
explanation: Inorder of any BST is sorted. The other sequences are the preorder (50 30 20 40 70), the postorder (20 40 30 70 50) and the level order (50 30 70 20 40).

question: Inserting 1, 2, 3, …, n in that order into an empty plain BST costs how much in total?
explanation: Sorted insertions build a chain: the i-th insert walks i − 1 nodes, 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) steps. Self-balancing trees like std::map avoid this.

question: Why does this validator accept the tree 5 with children 1 and 7, where 7 has a left child 4?
option_a: It checks children only, not all ancestors
option_b: It must use < and > instead of >= and <= in both checks
option_c: It forgets the base case for leaves
option_d: Nothing is wrong: that tree is in fact a valid BST
explanation: 4 is fine relative to its parent 7, but it lies in the right subtree of 5 and is smaller than 5. Pass an interval (lo, hi) down instead.

question: Deleting a node with two children using the inorder successor. Where is the successor, and why is it easy to remove?
option_a: It is the parent; swap the node with its parent directly
option_b: It is the right child, which always has no children
option_c: Leftmost in the right subtree; it has no left child
option_d: It is the rightmost node of the left subtree, a leaf
explanation: Being leftmost, the successor has no left child, so removing it is the leaf or one-child case. (The rightmost node of the left subtree is the predecessor, the mirror-image choice.)

question: BST: 20 with children 8 and 22; 8 has children 4 and 12; 12 has children 10 and 14. What is the successor of 13 (13 is not in the tree)?
explanation: The walk records 20 (go left), skips 8 (go right), skips 12 (go right), records 14 (go left, null). The last candidate, 14, is the smallest value greater than 13.

question: A BST iterator keeps a stack of left spines. What does a sequence of n calls to next() cost in total?
option_a: O(n), so each call is amortised O(1)
option_b: O(n log n), because each call pushes a spine
option_c: O(n·h), because a call may push h nodes
explanation: Each node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once over the whole iteration. A single call can push h nodes, but the total is n.

question: Why does the bounds validator use long long LLONG_MIN / LLONG_MAX instead of int INT_MIN / INT_MAX?
option_a: long long comparisons are faster than int ones on x86-64
option_b: Values may be INT_MIN/INT_MAX; strict int bounds reject them
option_c: It avoids recursion depth problems on degenerate chain trees
option_d: Because node values are stored as long long inside TreeNode
explanation: With bounds (INT_MIN, INT_MAX) and strict comparisons, a node holding INT_MIN fails val > lo. Wider bounds keep every int value legal.

question: Two-sum in a BST with a forward and a backward iterator: the current sum is smaller than the target. What do you do?
option_a: Advance the backward iterator to a smaller value
option_b: Restart both iterators from the root and try again
option_c: Push the root's right spine onto the forward stack
option_d: Advance the forward iterator to a larger value
explanation: The smallest unused value can't pair with anything, because it is already paired with the largest. Discard it by advancing the forward iterator.

question: The inorder of a BST with two swapped values is 1 5 3 4 2 6. Which nodes hold the wrong values?
explanation: The descents are 5 > 3 and 4 > 2. The first wrong node is the left element of the first descent (5); the second is the right element of the last descent (2).

question: range_sum on a BST: what should replace the comment?
explanation: The node and its whole left subtree are below lo, so only the right subtree can hold values in range. Returning 0 would miss them.

question: Which root does the balanced build use for the sorted range a[lo..hi] if mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2?
option_a: The lower middle when the length is even
option_b: The upper middle element when the length is even
option_c: The first element of the range, as in insertion
option_d: The median of the whole array every single time
explanation: For lo = 0, hi = 3, mid = 1: the lower of the two middle elements. (lo + hi + 1) / 2 would pick the upper one and build a different, equally balanced tree.
